prerequisites: Knowledge and comprehensive application of basic concepts of science and technology at Baccalaureate level (chemical, physical, mathematical and technical principles) required for the study of engineering.

Basic application of some strategies of the scientific methodology: locating, obtaining, analyzing and representing qualitative and quantitative information, interpreting, evaluating and communicating conclusions.

learning_outcomes.text: Develop knowledge of basic concepts about the general laws of mechanics, thermodynamics, fields and waves, and electromagnetism to be able to apply them significantly in the understanding of problem situations typical of engineering.
Know the fundamental concepts, laws, and principles of basic physics.
Distinguish the range of applicability of the fundamental concepts, laws, and principles of basic physics.
Apply significantly the fundamental concepts, laws, and principles of basic physics in different contexts.

Consistently employ procedural knowledge associated with scientific methodology in solving basic physics problems, both experimental and paper-based: perform qualitative analysis, formulate hypotheses, develop alternative strategies, and analyze results.
Make observations and qualitatively analyze the problem.
Formulate reasoned hypotheses.
Develop explanatory strategies.
Solve the problem.
Analyze the obtained results.
Work with information related to processes in basic physics, analyze and express ideas correctly using verbal, mathematical, and graphical language.
Search and analyze information.
Express ideas correctly both in writing and orally.
Use various systems of symbols or forms of representation: text, formulas, tables, graphs, and diagrams.
Work in a team to undertake cooperative tasks in the context of physics with colleagues: make proposals, analyze contributions from others, discuss ideas, and execute relevant actions.
Actively participate and assume individual responsibility in the group.
Collaborate using the tools of group work.
Adopt a favorable attitude towards learning the subject, being proactive, participative, and with a spirit of overcoming learning difficulties.
Show a responsible and committed attitude.
Show willingness to learn.
Use resources for autonomous work.

syllabus_topics: KINEMATICS: We will define the essence of measuring the position of a point in space and the concepts that define its motion, specializing the study in the most common movements. Finally, we will show the relationship between magnitudes determined by two observers between whom there is displacement but no rotation.

DYNAMICS OF A PARTICLE: We will begin the study with Newton's laws and their application limits, detailing forces that have special behaviors. We will define the angular momentum of a particle, its conservation, work, kinetic energy, potential energy, and their relationships.

DYNAMICS OF SYSTEMS OF PARTICLES: We will extend what was learned in the previous topic to the study of systems of several particles, highlighting the differences and applying it to the case of collisions and explosions.

RIGID BODY: After analyzing the general motion of a rigid body, we will focus on the study of its rotation, starting with angular momentum, work, and energy. We will study rolling motion and finally introduce the concepts of equilibrium and statics.

THERMODYNAMICS: After introducing a series of basic definitions and ideas, and the definition of an ideal gas, the concepts of heat and work, as well as internal energy, are addressed, which will allow us to establish the first principle of Thermodynamics, whose application will be especially analyzed in the case of closed systems consisting of ideal gases. Subsequently, the second principle of Thermodynamics and its different statements will be studied. Finally, cyclic processes and the efficiency of engines and refrigerators will be studied.

ELECTROSTATICS: This topic aims to show the electrical properties of matter, as well as to find the mathematical model that accounts for electrical interaction. After, given the lack of solutions of the previous model to solve certain problems, the concept of electric field is introduced, as well as its applications, and how to calculate it under any circumstances. Finally, electrostatic processes are addressed from an energetic approach, through the concept of potential, which allows us to have an alternative resolution strategy to that of using the concept of field, to solve problematic situations in the field of electrostatics.

APPLICATIONS OF THE ELECTRIC FIELD: This topic will serve to apply the concepts seen in the previous topic (field, potential, electrical energy, etc.) to practical cases from a technological point of view. We will introduce the concepts of capacitance and electric current. Finally, we will address the study of electrical circuits.

MAGNETIC FIELD: In this topic, we will analyze the sources of the magnetostatic field (magnets and moving charges), concluding that both are part of the same scheme; this will allow us to naturally delve into 'magnetization of matter'. Finally, we will address the study of a mathematical model that allows us to calculate magnetic fields under very specific symmetry conditions (Ampere's Law).

ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION: In the previous topics, only magnetic fields that do not vary with time have been considered. Now we address the study and applications of magnetic fields that do vary with time. We will deeply analyze the causes of electromagnetic induction, as well as the mathematical model (Faraday-Lenz law) that operationalizes the phenomenon of electromagnetic induction. We will conclude by analyzing some applications of this phenomenon and finally presenting Maxwell's laws.

WAVES: After introducing the essentials of simple harmonic motion, we will describe the basic concepts of waves and their types, specifically wave phenomena (interference, standing waves, diffraction), and finally the Doppler effect.
assessment_rules: For continuous assessment, a minimum of 5 out of 10 points is required from the sum of written tests, seminars, and laboratories. To pass, a minimum of 0.6 points in seminars and laboratories, and 1.2 points in each of the two blocks of written tests (or 0.9 points per block plus 1 point in seminars) are required. Students can opt for final assessment by taking a single comprehensive written exam worth 6 points, while seminars and laboratories will still be evaluated throughout the course, each worth 2 points. For the final assessment, the same minimum scores apply for seminars, laboratories, and each written exam block; otherwise, the final grade will be a maximum of 4.5 out of 10. For the extraordinary exam, students need a minimum of 5 points in total, with a written test (P3) worth 6 points, and separate written tests for seminars (2 points) and laboratories (2 points) if not passed during the course. Minimum scores of 0.6 points in seminars and laboratories, and 1.2 points in each written exam block are also required for the extraordinary exam; otherwise, the final grade will be a maximum of 4.5 out of 10.
